utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The case reference IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is my first Status Conference in this case, so I would be grateful if first of all counsel would introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appear for the Prosecution. But matters of detail will be dealt with by Ms. Romano on my right, who has the day-to-day conduct of the case, and we are also appearing today by Ms. Christina Moeller, who sits to her right, and our case manager on my left is Ms. Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. For Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon, Your Honour. Eugene O'Sullivan appearing on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. For Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, for Mr. Nikola Sainovic, attorney Vladimir Petrovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. And for Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Tomislav Visnjic for General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. The first matter that I am pleased to note is that pre-trial briefs have been lodged on behalf of each of the accused. There are a number of quite separate issues which I want to briefly address, but I don't think any gives rise to any particular difficulty that needs to be addressed today. An application is made for binding orders addressed to NATO states, and a decision has been taken to hear the submissions in that case in December. The view formed has been that it will take the best part of two full days to deal with that application. We have, therefore, allocated time on the afternoon of each of the 1st and 2nd of December and the whole of the 3rd of December in the hope that that can be dealt with then. Now, does any counsel have any comment to make on that arrangement? Thank you. Applications have been made on behalf of Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milutinovic for access to confidential material in the Milosevic proceedings. One matter remained outstanding. I've been able, with the assistance of Ms. Featherstone, to deal with that, and hopefully a decision disposing of the final outstanding matter will be issued in the next day or so. An application is made by the Prosecution for variation of protective measures for material provided pursuant to Rule 70. There's been no response on behalf of any of the accused in relation to that, and it may be that that is indicative of there being no need to consider this matter further and that the application can simply be granted. Is that the position so far as the Defence are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, in that event, an order will be drafted and issued dealing with that. Expert witnesses. There have been notices intimated on behalf of each accused in respect of the reports of eight expert witnesses. I can see that in the ordinary case, it would be appropriate simply to leave the matter of how to deal with expert reports and witnesses to the trial. But two of the experts in this case have already been the subject of decisions excluding their evidence completely, the expert Torkildsen and the expert Kristan. In the case of Kristan, I suppose his evidence was not excluded completely, but so far as it's relevant to this trial it was excluded completely. And it struck me that there might be some benefit in inviting the Prosecution to respond to these notices with a view to considering whether the position can be dealt with and clarified in advance of the trial. And if the Prosecution were to be invited to respond in respect of two of the experts, then it struck me also that there would be no harm in inviting them to respond in relation to all eight, bearing in mind that substantial submissions are made on behalf of each of the accused in relation to all the expert reports. Now, I turn first of all to Ms. Romano for reaction to the suggestion that the Prosecution might be invited to respond to the notices which have been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Prosecution doesn't see any problem in addressing this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And so far as timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I will have to ask at least maybe what, two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far as counsel for the accused are concerned, is there any comment to make on that, to dissuade me from following that course or reducing the time or on any other point? No. Very well. What I -- Ms. Featherstone, is it the appropriate course to make an order following today's hearing or simply to make an oral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think what I'll do is make an order requiring the Prosecution to respond to the three notices in 14 days, and no doubt counsel for the accused, if they consider it appropriate, will invite the Chamber to receive any further comments that they wish to make in the light of these responses. I note that there is some uncertainty about the role of the Prosecution in continuous reporting of the situation in relation to Rule -- the disclosure of Rule 68 material. It may be that that has been resolved, but as matters stood when I was preparing for this, it did seem that the Prosecution position was that their obligation to continue to report was now at an end. It's not entirely clear to me that that is so. Is there anything you wish to say on that matter, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, it's our position that in light of the Rule change, most recently introduced Rule 68, where the whole Rule was made subject to the provisions of Rule 70, there is no duty now of any kind falling on the Prosecution in one of these cases to reveal anything to the accused or to the Court about its dealings with Rule 70 material that it judges may have a Rule 68 component. In those circumstances, and as a matter of theory, in this case, there would be no justification, it could be argued, for continuing the practice of 68 reporting that I can't remember now whether it was the Court introduced it or whether we actually volunteered it, but one way or another I can remember instigating the process of Rule 68 reporting outside the provisions of the Rules at an earlier occasion in the Milosevic case, and I think the practice spilled over into this case. So we have a system of reporting that is, I think, outside, strictly outside, the Rules in which we've sought to help the parties, and it's a practice in relation to 68, 70 material that is now more generous or has been more generous than the Rules now require.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean you're saying it's not the Rule change that makes the Prosecution take this line, but that simply awakened a desire to reduce the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I think the Rule change freezes without doubt of any need to report -- if we're reporting at all, the Rule change freezes of any need to report on Rule 70 material that has an arguable Rule 68 component. Now, the question is, since we've -- or one of the issues is: Since we have, as a matter of fact, under the reporting mechanism that I suspect we introduced being keeping parties informed about what in this case we've been doing about material that is both Rule 68 and Rule 70, should we continue to do so, in this case, although we'll do something different in other cases? There's no prejudice, of course, to the accused in our ceasing to report, because information about what we are doing with Rule 70 providers in respect to material that is Rule 70 and Rule 68 is of no utility to them in any event, so not having the information doesn't help them, or having it doesn't help them. But nevertheless having said all that, we don't see any particular problem in this case without prejudice to other cases in just carrying on the process of reporting, although, as we say, we don't think it's of any relevance to, nor can it be any utility to the defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm obliged to you for that, Mr. Nice, so I'll simply note that the practice will at least continue until this case goes to trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should just like to respond to what Mr. Nice said a moment ago, briefly and I'll start by going back into history, if I may. The Defence of General Ojdanic, on the 30th of October, 2002, submitted, filed a request --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you go any further, can I be clear on the purpose of this submission? The Prosecution position is no change so far as this case is concerned, and it's certainly not my intention to make a decision in principle about the point that might affect other cases if that's not required to advance the present one. Is there a separate point that arises for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If they continue to supply us with information as they have been doing so far, we will be quite satisfied with that. But as I understood it, and according to what was written down in their eighth report on disclosure, I think the position there was contrary to what you've just said, or what Mr. Nice just said, and that is why I wanted to make a brief comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Visnjic, that Mr. Nice has, for the purposes of the present case, departed from what was said in the eighth report, without prejudice to the position the Prosecution might take in any other case. So you needn't worry about it so far as the present case is concerned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I have not noted any further matters. Is there any other procedural or technical issue that the Prosecution or Defence wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Will Your Honour just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing to raise, but since it's always rather intriguing to see somebody discuss something and want to know what they were actually thinking about, I don't see any reason not to at least mention what is in my mind, and that is whether this case, certainly by the time it starts, is one where there will be any use, utility, desirability, in having computerised systems of information and evidence management that can be common to the three interested organs of the trial, the Bench, Prosecution, and Defence. Our computer systems are advancing, and I know that the practices differ as between chambers and the Prosecution, and it may be that it's something that at some stage it would be sensible to give some thought to, perhaps later 65 ter conferences or Status Conferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps at the next 65 ter conference, it might be an appropriate time to raise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm quite confident that if there is within any trial the potential to harmonise systems for managing material, there may be very great savings in both costs and substantial increases in efficiencies of presentations and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nice. Does any Defence counsel have any other matter to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Nothing at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand it's the practice at these Status Conferences to give to the accused the opportunity to mention any matter that they do wish to raise. The practice I intend to follow is to invite counsel to indicate if there is anything that they do wish to raise about the conditions of the accused or any other relevant matter. If you decide that it's appropriate to raise any such matter, then it's for you to decide whether you make the submission to me or the comment, or you invite your client to do so. But I will direct that inquiry always to counsel rather than to clients directly. So is there any other matter of even a general nature or about conditions generally that you wish to comment upon at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Nothing on behalf of Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Sainovic and on behalf of the Defence, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not have anything to raise either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you to counsel. That brings the proceedings at this Status Conference to an end. The date of the next one, I think we should fix upon now, and I have in mind the 13th of January. So I take it in the absence of dissent, that will be the date of the next Status Conference. Sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 13th of January is New Year's Eve, according to the Orthodox Christian calendar. I just wanted to say that, and we would highly appreciate it if that would not be a working day, so that we could meet some other time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please excuse my insensitivity on that. What alternative do you propose?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any date after the 15th, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The conference has to be held on or before the 14th, and we don't resume, I think, until the 10th. So there's a limited selection of dates available.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. May I just consult my colleagues for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand also that with agreement it could be postponed until the beginning of the following week. If that's the proposal you want to make, then I'm open to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Precisely, Your Honour. That is what we had wished to ask for, just a brief extension. We agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case, I think the 18th of January would be appropriate. So the next Status Conference will be this time, and on the 18th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
